name: Duration neglect
statement: Retrospective evaluations of an episode barely move with how long it lasted, so an experience of the same intensity is remembered as no worse for going on longer.
meaning: The claim is about weight, not about awareness. People can say roughly how long something took and still give that length almost no role when asked how good or how bad the whole thing was. Duration neglect is bundled with the peak–end rule, entry 76, and the two are separable. The peak–end rule says which moments carry the verdict; duration neglect says the number of moments does not. Each has failed while the other held: in three studies of meals the length of exposure was neglected and the peak, the first dish and the last dish predicted nothing. Duration neglect is also the older half of the pair, named four months before the cold-pressor study that made the peak–end rule famous. Where it holds, the memory of an episode and the sum of what was lived come apart, so a person choosing by memory can pick the episode that contained more total discomfort.

origin.who: Barbara L. Fredrickson and Daniel Kahneman
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper names the phenomenon and defines it as little or no independent effect of duration on retrospective evaluations of affective episodes. The first demonstration was Varey and Kahneman in 1992, where people judged another person's discomfort from written lists of ratings. Fredrickson and Kahneman report that duration was significant there and added 3% of additional variance, and that study is described here through their account of it.

evidence: Thirty-two students at the University of California, Berkeley, aged 16 to 35, watched six pleasant and six aversive film clips, each in a short or a long version, and marked a 100-mm line after each one. Aversive clips ran 28.8 seconds on average when short and 84.2 seconds when long. Mean evaluations of the aversive clips moved from 55.18 to 65.33 with length, and the mean within-subject biserial correlation between duration and evaluation was .26. Duration correlated .41 with peak affect and .32 with end affect, so length shifted the moment-by-moment experience more than it shifted the verdict. With the sum of peak and end affect held constant, the mean partial correlation between duration and the evaluation of aversive clips was -.02, t(30) = 0.18. Pleasant clips showed no reliable duration effect, and the long versions of the puppy film and the waves film were rated below the short ones. At the close of that session the same subjects estimated the long versions at about twice the length of the short ones, so they knew what they were setting aside. Study 2 showed the same clips to 96 students who ranked them at the end of the session. Duration correlated .24 with the rankings of aversive clips when people knew the ranking task in advance and .12 when they ranked from memory, a difference at t(94) = 1.90, p < .10. One number from the colonoscopy work reached print only later. Eighty-nine of the colonoscopy patients were re-interviewed about a month later and asked to choose between a future colonoscopy and a stomach X-ray. Ariely, Kahneman and Loewenstein report that the biserial correlation between that choice and the duration of the procedure was .01, and that the result was left out of the 1996 paper by oversight.

replication.headline: Duration comes out near zero when episodes are rated one at a time, and carries about the weight of the ending when the same sounds are judged by a decision.
replication.detail: Ariely and Loewenstein put 27 annoying sounds through four evaluation methods. The sounds lasted 10, 15 or 22.5 seconds and varied in loudness and in shape. Each participant's evaluations were regressed on peak, end and duration. The mean standardised weight on duration was 0.122 when sounds were rated one at a time and 0.334 when people named the lowest payment they would take to hear a sound again. It was 0.266 when each sound was rated against a fixed standard and 0.304 when they chose between a sound and that standard. Peak carried 0.437, 0.416, 0.494 and 0.357 across the same four. The rating method used in most earlier work is the one that produced neglect. Liersch and McKenzie redrew Varey and Kahneman's number lists as bar graphs and ran 113 students, 37 on lists, 38 on graphs and 38 on a modified list. Evaluations differed between every duration level for the graphs, p < .001, and between none of them for the plain lists. The modified list, which showed the maximum possible length, separated only the 15 and 35 minute episodes, p = .02, and its pattern of neglect did not differ from the plain list, p = .59 for the interaction. Graphs left most people adding where lists left them averaging. Schreiber and Kahneman report that the effects of sound duration and intensity are additive across trials. Where duration stays out of view the neglect holds. Rode, Rozin and Durlach found it across three studies of meals, with no peak, primacy or recency effect beside it. Doubling the favourite course moved the imagined meals of 20 people by 0.41 and 0.44 on a rating line, t(16) = 0.59 and t(17) = 0.12, against the 3 millimetres their own arithmetic predicted if duration counted. In a restaurant it left another 20 diners rating the doubled meal lower rather than higher, by 3.4, t(19) = 0.71. Their first study ran 173 undergraduates through meals made of jelly beans. Kemp, Burt and Furneaux collected 49 holiday records from 47 students by daily text message, on holidays of 4 to 14 days. Recalled overall happiness correlated .06 with length at the first recall test and -.30 at the second, which 27 people sat. Neither correlation carries a significance mark in the paper's tables, and its text says neither test showed a significant relationship between the duration of the holiday and the rating of overall happiness. Alaybek and colleagues pooled 174 effect sizes and put the effect of duration at essentially nil. Weingarten, Zauberman and Diehl report seven studies that reproduce the direct neglect and find duration reaching evaluations indirectly, by changing where the peak and the end fall. The largest recent test of the peak–end rule, an experience-sampling study of 1,889 people, sits at entry 76 and does not analyse duration.

study.cite: Ariely, D., & Loewenstein, G. (2000). When does duration matter in judgment and decision making? Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 129(4), 508-523.

limits: No figure is quoted here for the pooled duration effect. The 2022 meta-analysis is paywalled and its abstract gives duration as essentially nil without a number. The 2024 corrigendum to it still could not be read on 17 August 2026: the publisher refused every route tried, and Unpaywall lists no repository copy. Ariely and Loewenstein's participants section names undergraduates at Duke University and at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology without counting them, so no sample size is given here. Their scanned copy carries no text layer, and their regression table was read off page images. Their sounds ran at most 22.5 seconds. Liersch and McKenzie are read from the authors' accepted draft dated July 2008; the published version is closed at Unpaywall. Schreiber and Kahneman and Weingarten and colleagues are read from their PubMed abstracts, and no effect size is taken from either. Searches for open copies of those two on 17 August 2026 covered Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, author and departmental pages, SSRN and web search. The 1996 colonoscopy paper was not obtained, and entry 76 records the same failure against the same venues. Its procedures ran from 4 to 67 minutes according to Ariely, Kahneman and Loewenstein, while Fredrickson and Kahneman describe an earlier report of the same work with 101 patients and a range of 4 to 69 minutes. Varey and Kahneman in 1992 is closed at Unpaywall and is described here at one remove. One unpublished correlation is characterised twice in the joint comment, and the two characterisations differ. Kahneman calls the link between those colonoscopy choices and the average of peak and end marginally significant at p < .03, one-tailed. Ariely and Loewenstein call it marginally correlated at p < .06, two-tailed, and worth under 4% of the variance in choice. The longest episodes tested in any source here are holidays of two weeks. Searches for later duration-specific work on 17 August 2026 covered Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex and web search, and turned up nothing after 2022.
misreadings: The most common error is to treat duration neglect and the peak–end rule as one finding, so that a failure of either is read as a failure of both. Rode and colleagues separate them cleanly: duration was neglected while peak, primacy and recency did nothing. A second error is to read neglect as not noticing. Fredrickson and Kahneman's subjects judged the long clips to be about twice as long as the short ones, and the authors describe duration as an attribute people know and consider important in the abstract. A third is to treat the size of the effect as a property of people rather than of the question. Ariely and Loewenstein moved the weight on duration from 0.122 to 0.334 by changing nothing but the response mode. A fourth is to cite the cold-pressor choice as proof. Ariely, Kahneman and Loewenstein agree in print that the violations of dominance in that study do not by themselves demonstrate duration neglect, since heavy weight on the ending produces the same choice. Their joint statement is the shortest correction available: none of the three authors expects complete duration neglect when attention is drawn to duration, explicitly or otherwise.
